extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for forming, naming, and defining general conceptions used in induction: how to choose appropriate and clear classes/names and how to construct definitions that support scientific generalization. Focuses on the intellectual habits and linguistic principles that make induction possible and reliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of a conception
rubrics_metrics.description: The conception must correspond to a real agreement among the phenomena; it should bring together instances that agree in particulars relevant to the law or property under investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriateness is relative to the object or purpose in view: a conception suited to one inquiry may be inappropriate to another. Example anti-pattern: classing animals merely by color yields legitimate but often trivial conceptions (white animal, black animal) that are inappropriate for studying structure or habits; by contrast, classification by skeleton structure or integument leads to conceptions more 'appropriate' to biological inquiries. An 'appropriate' conception should extend across the relevant cases of the phenomenon and exclude cases that do not exhibit the phenomenon; otherwise the conception will mislead (Aristotle's 'natural motion' example shows a conception that includes irrelevant cases and excludes pertinent ones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness (precision/determinacy) of conception
rubrics_metrics.description: A conception must be clear: we must know exactly in what the agreement consists; the resemblance must be analyzed and accurately remembered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearness requires careful observation, extensive experience, and an accurate memory. It does not require knowledge of all common properties, only that one knows exactly why items are classed together and that the conception remains determinate (not fluctuating from day to day) except when consciously revised due to new knowledge. Anti-patterns: vague, fluctuating, or merely felt resemblances; having only a general feeling of resemblance without specifying the points of agreement (ship vs frigate example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptions must correspond to real classes (real distinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A class must be a 'real class' — the things it includes must really agree in certain particulars and differ from other things in those particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a name or class does not correspond to any real agreement, it is inapplicable and will not support induction. A person without clear ideas habitually groups things with no common properties or cannot state the common properties when challenged. Ensuring a real distinction often requires feature-by-feature comparison and sometimes inductive work to reveal unobvious agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance/appropriateness relative to purpose (theoretical or practical)
rubrics_metrics.description: The properties included in a conception should be those which help toward the specific purpose of inquiry — either deep properties for theoretical understanding or properties closely connected to the particular attribute under study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all true agreements are equally valuable: prefer those that go deepest into the nature of the things or are most closely connected to the property under investigation. A conception may be 'clear' but still inappropriate for a given inquiry if it does not highlight the properties relevant to the problem at hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness to revision; avoid permanent acquiescence to premature conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: General conceptions formed without thorough knowledge are necessary provisional tools, but they become impediments when permanently accepted despite being wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Premature ('Bacon’s notiones temerè à rebus abstractæ') conceptions are acceptable as steps toward better understanding, but intellectual progress requires willingness to alter conceptions when further knowledge or better theory shows them to be wrong. Historical anti-pattern: ancients' persistent wrong classifications in physics or persistent errors in morals and politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual habits required: attentive observation, active comparison, and scientific imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: The chances of hitting on appropriate and clear conceptions depend on the activity and accuracy of observing and comparing faculties and on the scientific imagination for forming useful hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate habits of minute observation and careful comparison, broad experience, and memory. For hidden or non-obvious agreements, prior conceptions or hypotheses and the ability to mentally recombine known elements are necessary (e.g., planetary orbits case). These are skills often developed outside pure logic (art of education).

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming as an instrument of induction (general names as permanent signs)
rubrics_metrics.description: General names (universals) are indispensable for recording and recalling uniformities discovered by induction; they serve as artificial memory and as the medium for conveying general propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While very simple inductive inferences between particulars can occur without language (brute induction), advanced induction (comparison of many observations, experiments in varying circumstances) requires general signs. Names fix uniformities so they can be remembered, communicated, and used as formulas to make subsequent inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every general name must have a steadily fixed and precisely determined meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: A philosophical language needs general names whose meanings (connotations) are fixed and knowable so they can reliably serve as instruments of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The meaning of a general connotative name resides in its connotation (the attributes it implies). To give names a precise meaning is to fix the attributes connoted by each concrete general name and the denotation of the corresponding abstract. Technical terms are easier; common-use terms require analysis of current usage to ascertain and fix their connotation (examples: 'animal', abstract 'sensation'/'voluntary motion'; problematic common terms: 'civilized', 'honor', 'gentleman').

rubrics_metrics.name: There should be a name wherever one is needed
rubrics_metrics.description: A philosophical language should supply a name wherever there is something important to be designated which it is useful to express.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having an appropriate name for important concepts facilitates recording and communicating general truths; absence of names impedes expression of useful distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of existing names should be fixed in accordance with received use where practicable
rubrics_metrics.description: When fixing the connotation of a name already in use, prefer meanings that do not conflict with generally received propositions in which the term figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid semantic revolutions that would render common propositions false or unintelligible; the fixed connotation should agree (as far as it goes) with the loose, fluctuating connotation already possessed by the term. A definition should not require rupture of strong associations created by familiar usage (example: one would have little chance of convincing people to call North American Indians 'civilized' if that required overturning entrenched usages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Select definitional attributes that are marks of many others or are causally significant
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple common properties exist, choose for the definition those attributes which experience or deduction shows many others depend upon, or which are sure marks of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer properties that are well-known and commonly predicated of the class but filter them toward those that serve best to mark the class and allow further inference. Good definitions facilitate inference: they should be tied to properties from which many other properties follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meanings of terms in use are to be ascertained, not arbitrarily assigned
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper task is to discover and fix the connotation a term already has via usage and associated propositions, not to impose an arbitrary connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To define a name actually in use requires investigation of the existing associations and propositions involving that name. Fixing a connotation often involves feature-by-feature comparison of denoted objects and can itself be an inductive operation. One should not define a term in a way that makes received assertions inadmissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explication/unfolding of conceptions (definition as analysis of the common attributes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explication consists in ascertaining, better than before, the particulars in which phenomena classed together agree — 'unfolding' the general conception in virtue of which they are so classed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many scientific controversies take the form of disputes about definitions because definitions tacitly assume propositions to be expressed. Good explication requires examination of the properties of things and sometimes resolving empirical controversies (examples: measures of force, specific/latent heat, definition of mineral species, organization). Definitions and their disputes acquire real value because they relate to propositions about the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions are not mere matters of arbitrary choice but are tied to propositions and theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Controversies about definitions are important because each definition is chosen with an eye to certain propositions and theoretical usefulness; they are thus substantive issues about truth, not mere verbal quibbles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When disputing or proposing definitions, make explicit the propositions and theoretical aims that give the definition value. A definition's correctness or usefulness depends on the propositions it is meant to express and the degree to which it supports true generalizations.
